Session routine.long:
A session routine is the fixed sequence a trader runs before, during and after each trading session: the same preparation, the same checks, the same shutdown, regardless of mood or recent results.

The routine's job is to move decisions out of the moment. Before the session: what is on the calendar, what levels matter, what setups are permitted today, what is the loss limit. During: only what the plan allows. After: log the trades, note the state you were in, close the platform. Every one of those items is trivial; the compound effect of doing them identically for months is not, because the routine is what stands between a plan and the improvisation that replaces plans under stress.

The evidence for routines is strongest in every other performance field — aviation and surgery formalised checklists precisely because skilled people skip steps under load — and trading borrows the logic directly.

Where people get fooled: keeping the routine while results are good and dropping it in drawdown, which is backwards. The routine exists for the losing stretch; abandoning it then is removing the guardrail at the corner. A routine only followed when it feels unnecessary was never a routine.
Session routine.usage: Generally a fixed pre/during/post sequence run identically every session; its value shows up in the stretches where it feels pointless.

Trade log fields.long:
Trade log fields are the columns a journal captures for every trade: date, instrument, direction, entry, stop, exit, size, R result, setup name, and whatever context the review process actually uses.

The design principle is that fields exist to answer questions. R per setup type answers which setups earn their place. Planned-versus-actual entry answers whether execution leaks money. A rule-followed flag separates the system's performance from the trader's interference — two numbers that diverge in the most instructive way possible. A one-line reason and an emotional-state note make later pattern-finding possible without trusting memory, which rewrites history freely.

Fewer fields, always filled, beat many fields abandoned by Thursday. A log that takes ninety seconds per trade survives; one that takes ten minutes becomes fiction within a month.

Where people get fooled: logging outcomes but not conditions. A journal of dates and profits can only say whether you made money, which the account already says. The fields that pay are the ones that let you group trades — by setup, by session, by state — because the groups are where a specific, fixable problem finally becomes visible.
Trade log fields.usage: Typically the minimum set that lets trades be grouped and compared later; designed around the review questions, not around completeness.

Review cadence.long:
Review cadence is the schedule on which trading is examined: commonly a brief daily log check, a weekly session review, and a monthly or quarterly look at whether the whole approach is earning its keep.

The layering matters because different questions need different sample sizes. Daily review can only sensibly ask about execution — did I follow the plan — because one day's results are noise. Weekly review can spot recurring leaks: a setup repeatedly mistimed, a session that consistently costs money. Only the monthly and quarterly layers have enough trades to say anything about expectancy, and even they are thin for most retail frequencies. Matching the question to the sample is the discipline; asking is my strategy working after four trades is how good systems get abandoned and bad ones kept.

The cadence also caps tinkering. Changes made mid-week in response to two losses are reactions; the same change proposed at the scheduled review, against the logged evidence, is a decision.

Where people get fooled: reviewing intensely after losses and not at all after wins. Both halves are wrong — loss-triggered review happens in exactly the state that reads noise as signal, and unreviewed winning streaks are where rule-drift quietly compounds until the market audits it for you.
Review cadence.usage: Generally layered — daily for execution, weekly for leaks, monthly-plus for expectancy — with each question matched to a sample that can answer it.

Strategy retirement.long:
Strategy retirement is the deliberate shutdown of a strategy that no longer earns its place — with pre-defined criteria, a written record of why, and the discipline not to sneak it back three weeks later.

The hard part is separating a dead edge from an ordinary drawdown, and the honest answer is that no test does this cleanly. What helps: criteria set in advance, when the strategy was healthy — a maximum drawdown, a longest-tolerable losing stretch, a performance floor over a rolling window — so the decision was made by a calm version of you. Structural evidence beats statistical evidence: if the mechanism the strategy exploited has visibly changed — the spread widened, the participants left, the product died — retirement needs less data than the equity curve alone would demand.

Retired is also not deleted. The strategy, its record and the reason for shutdown go to the archive, because conditions recur and a documented past beats a fresh search.

Where people get fooled: retiring at the bottom of a normal drawdown and reviving at the top of the next lucky run — a cycle that converts a breakeven strategy into a reliably losing one by systematically holding it during its worst stretches and benching it during its best.
Strategy retirement.usage: Generally governed by criteria written while the strategy was healthy; structural change justifies faster exits than equity-curve evidence alone.

Position reconciliation.long:
Position reconciliation is checking that what you think you hold matches what the broker says you hold: every position, every order, every balance, agreed line by line between your records and the platform's.

Manual traders need a light version — a end-of-session glance confirming nothing is open that should be closed, no order resting that should be cancelled. Automated trading needs the full ritual, because software fails in ways that leave the system's internal picture and the broker's reality quietly different: a fill missed during a disconnect, a partial fill recorded as complete, a cancel that never landed. Every automated blowup story includes the phrase the system thought.

The check is mechanical: pull the broker's state, compare with the strategy's state, alarm on any difference, and never let the system trade while the two disagree. The comparison costs seconds; the class of error it catches costs accounts.

Where people get fooled: assuming an absence of errors because none have surfaced. Unreconciled discrepancies do not announce themselves — they sit as a phantom position or an orphaned stop until a volatile day monetises the difference. The Knight Capital collapse in 2012 was, at its core, a reconciliation failure wearing a deployment error.
Position reconciliation.usage: Generally an end-of-session check for manual traders and a continuous requirement for automated ones; the system never trades while its state and the broker's disagree.

Backup and redundancy.long:
Backup and redundancy is the boring insurance layer of trading operations: a second way to close a position when the first fails, and copies of everything that would hurt to lose.

The priority list is short and ordered by damage. First, the ability to flatten positions when the platform dies mid-trade: the broker's phone dealing number written down somewhere not on the computer, the mobile app installed and logged in, and — for leveraged positions — a stop resting at the broker rather than only on your machine. Second, the data: journal, strategy records, configuration, backed up automatically to somewhere that survives the laptop. Third, connectivity and power to the degree your holding period justifies — a scalper needs a phone hotspot ready; a swing trader mostly needs the resting stops.

None of this earns anything, which is why it competes badly for attention against anything that might.

Where people get fooled: discovering the gaps live. The platform freezes during the news spike — that is when the phone number matters, and when it turns out the app was never logged in, the number needs a security code that arrives by email, and the position is doing what positions do in fast markets: moving. Redundancy is only real if it has been tested on a calm day.
Backup and redundancy.usage: Generally: a tested second route to flatten positions, resting stops at the broker, and automatic backups of records; rehearsed before it is needed.

Capital allocation.long:
Capital allocation is the split of trading capital across strategies, markets and reserves: how much runs the tested system, how much funds experiments, how much stays out of the market entirely.

The useful frame treats allocations as decisions with owners and review dates rather than drift. A common structure: the bulk behind whatever has survived testing, a small fixed research budget for unproven ideas — sized so total loss is an acceptable tuition bill — and an untouched reserve that makes ruin arithmetic impossible. The research allocation matters most psychologically: experiments funded from a budget get evaluated; experiments funded from the main account get defended.

Allocation also encodes honesty about capacity. Doubling capital behind a strategy because it had a good quarter is a decision that should have to pass the same evidence bar as any other claim — one good quarter clears no bar at all.

Where people get fooled: allocation by recency. Money migrates toward whatever performed last month and away from whatever struggled, which systematically buys strategies at their peaks and abandons them at their troughs — the same behaviour that damages fund investors, run privately at higher speed. The written allocation, changed only at scheduled reviews, is the defence.
Capital allocation.usage: Generally a written split — core, research, reserve — changed at scheduled reviews rather than drifting with recent results.

Withdrawal policy.long:
A withdrawal policy is a pre-decided rule for taking money out of the trading account: how much, on what schedule, under what conditions — written down before the profits it applies to exist.

The policy solves a real problem: without one, no result triggers a withdrawal. Winning feels like the wrong time — the account is compounding, why interrupt it — and losing feels impossible, because withdrawing would lock in the drawdown. So accounts ride round trips from initial deposit to peak and back, and the trader who was up substantially banks none of it. A rule as simple as a fixed percentage of net new profits each quarter converts paper outcomes into the only kind that ultimately counts.

Withdrawals also function as measurement. An account that has returned more than its deposits is in unambiguous profit regardless of what the equity curve claims; prop traders live by payout received, not dashboard balance, for the same reason.

Where people get fooled: compounding as a reason to never withdraw. The arithmetic of compounding is real, but it applies to strategies with a durable edge — and the whole question is whether yours is one. A withdrawal schedule is the hedge against the answer being no: whatever the eventual verdict, some of the good period left the table.
Withdrawal policy.usage: Generally a fixed schedule and fraction decided in advance; profit that has been withdrawn is the only profit that is settled.

Drawdown protocol.long:
A drawdown protocol is a written, tiered response to losing streaks, agreed with yourself in advance: at each depth of drawdown, a specific action — reduce size, pause a strategy, stop entirely — happens automatically.

The design logic is that judgement degrades exactly when it is most needed. A trader ten percent down is anxious, tempted to press, and highly motivated to reinterpret rules. The protocol was written by the calm version, so the impaired version only has to comply, not decide. A workable ladder: at one threshold, halve size; at the next, trade the minimum while continuing to log; at the final one, flat for a fixed period and a full review before restarting. The size reductions also directly slow the arithmetic of ruin while the cause — variance, decay, or self-inflicted — is diagnosed.

The restart rules matter as much as the shutdown rules: what evidence permits size to return, over what schedule. Otherwise the protocol ends with a revenge-sized re-entry.

Where people get fooled: writing the protocol and renegotiating it live — this drawdown is different, the setup is too good, the rule was for other situations. Every drawdown is different and none of them are; the protocol's entire value is that it does not take the current one's word for it.
Drawdown protocol.usage: Generally a pre-written ladder — cut size, minimum size, stop — with explicit restart criteria; written calm, executed impaired.

Journaling the near-misses.long:
Journaling the near-misses is recording the trades that almost happened and the disasters that almost did: the rule violation that got away with it, the setup skipped from fear, the fat-finger caught at the confirmation screen, the stop nearly moved.

The practice imports a core idea from aviation and medical safety: incidents and accidents share causes, so the incidents — vastly more numerous — are the cheap data. A rewarded rule break is the most important near-miss in trading, because the reward trains repetition and the repetition eventually meets the outcome the rule existed to prevent. Logged, it is visible as the leading indicator it is; unlogged, it is remembered as a win.

Skipped valid setups are the other half — hesitation is a performance leak the profit column never shows, and only a record of what should have been taken reveals its cost.

Where people get fooled: journals that only contain executed trades. That dataset cannot see drift while it is still cheap: by the time rule-breaking shows up in results, the habit is months old and has a track record of its own to defend it. The near-miss log catches the same failure at the stage where fixing it costs a sentence of writing instead of a drawdown.
Journaling the near-misses.usage: Generally a log of violations that worked, setups skipped and errors caught in time — the leading indicators the P&L column shows too late.

Version control for strategies.long:
Version control for strategies is keeping every change to a strategy's rules recorded and dated — what changed, when, and why — so the strategy's history is a sequence of identifiable versions rather than a blur of adjustments.

The payoff is attribution. When results shift, the first question is whether the market changed or the strategy did, and without versioning that question has no answer: memory smooths the edits into always having traded it this way. With versioning, performance attaches to versions — version three earned its record, version four is two weeks old and owns nothing yet. That distinction stops the commonest laundering in trading, where a modified strategy quietly inherits the track record of its ancestor.

The tooling can be as heavy as git or as light as a dated page per version, but the rule is the same either way: any change to entries, exits, sizing or filters creates a new version, and the version trades long enough to earn its own evidence.

Where people get fooled: continuous small tweaks, none of which feels like a new version. Each is a reasonable refinement; the sum is a strategy that has never actually been tested, wearing the confidence of a record produced by rules that no longer exist.
Version control for strategies.usage: Generally: date every rule change and attach performance to versions, so edits cannot inherit a predecessor's track record.

Trading as a business.long:
Trading as a business is the frame that treats trading like any other enterprise: known costs, measured revenue, defined processes, capital requirements, and periodic honest accounts — rather than as a hobby with money in it.

The frame earns its keep through the questions it forces. What does this operation cost to run — data, platform, commissions, and the hours it consumes at what those hours are worth elsewhere? What is the realistic revenue given the capital and the measured expectancy, and is that number worth the costs? What is the plan when the primary strategy stops working — the business equivalent of a key product dying? Businesses that cannot answer these fold; traders who cannot answer them often continue for years, because nobody sends them the invoice for their own time.

The frame also right-sizes expectations: a business plan projecting the returns implied by turning five thousand dollars into a living would be laughed out of any bank.

Where people get fooled: adopting the aesthetic instead of the accounting — the desk, the screens, the LLC — while the actual books, had they existed, would show a money-losing operation subsidised by a salary. The business frame is a discipline of arithmetic, not a costume.
Trading as a business.usage: Generally a framing device: full cost accounting including your time, realistic revenue projection, and a plan for the main product dying.

Opportunity cost of time.long:
The opportunity cost of time is what the hours spent trading would have earned elsewhere — in paid work, in skills that compound, in the life that happens off the screens. It is the largest unbilled expense in most retail trading operations.

The arithmetic is uncomfortable and worth doing once a year. Hours per week on trading and its research, multiplied by what those hours command in your actual profession, is the operation's true labour cost; a trading profit that looks respectable can price the hours behind it below any wage you would accept from an employer. Small accounts make the problem structural: even an excellent return on limited capital divides into a poor hourly rate, which is why the honest question for most people is not can I trade profitably but is this the best use of what these hours could build.

Screen time also has a second cost the ledger misses: hours watching charts mid-session are hours in a state that produces impulsive trades, so past a point, more time spent actively degrades the result.

Where people get fooled: counting only cash costs. The subscription and commissions are visible; the two thousand annual hours are not, and a hobby that loses a little money while consuming a working year of attention is far more expensive than its statement shows.
Opportunity cost of time.usage: Generally computed yearly: hours consumed times their market value, set against measured trading profit; small accounts rarely survive the comparison.

Skill vs luck attribution.long:
Skill-versus-luck attribution is the discipline of asking, for any trading result, how much was decision quality and how much was noise — and accepting that over small samples the answer is mostly noise, in both directions.

Trading sits far toward the luck-dominated end of the activity spectrum in the short run, alongside poker and away from chess. The practical consequences are concrete. A month's results — good or bad — carry almost no information about skill at retail trade frequencies; the sample is too small and the variance too high. Attribution therefore has to run through process: was the plan followed, were the trades from the tested playbook, was sizing right? Those questions have answers at any sample size. Outcome-based attribution, meanwhile, teaches confidently and wrongly — it promotes the reckless winner and demotes the disciplined loser, exactly backwards from what the long run rewards.

The structural fix is separating the two ledgers: an execution score you control completely, and an outcome record that needs hundreds of trades before it testifies.

Where people get fooled: asymmetric attribution — wins credited to skill, losses to bad luck. It is the default setting of human confidence, it feels like reasonable self-belief from inside, and it guarantees the feedback loop that should correct errors instead reinforces them.
Skill vs luck attribution.usage: Generally resolved through process metrics at small samples and outcome metrics only at large ones; the asymmetric version is the default failure.

Definition of done.long:
A definition of done is the pre-agreed standard a piece of trading work must meet before it counts as finished: what a tested strategy means, what a completed review includes, what qualifies research as decided rather than drifting.

Borrowed from software practice, the concept attacks a specific failure: work that ends when enthusiasm does. A backtest is not done because it produced a chart; done might mean costs included, out-of-sample split respected, parameter neighbourhood checked, result written up with a verdict. A trade review is not done because the trades were reread; done might mean every trade tagged, rule compliance scored, one action item extracted or explicitly none. Written standards make done checkable — and make not done visible, which is the point.

The standard also protects against the opposite failure, gold-plating: research that never concludes because one more test always suggests itself. Done means the verdict gets written with the evidence available and the question closes.

Where people get fooled: the drifting definition — done meaning whatever state the work reached when attention moved on. Every abandoned half-test then reads as done in memory, and decisions get built on work that met no standard, carrying confidence borrowed from work that did.
Definition of done.usage: Generally a written completion standard per work type — tested, reviewed, decided — so unfinished work cannot masquerade as evidence.

Research backlog.long:
A research backlog is the ordered list of trading questions worth investigating, each captured as a testable item with a reason it earned a place — the pipeline that decides what gets attention next.

The backlog's first job is capture with deferral: mid-session is when ideas arrive and the worst time to pursue them, so the backlog is where they go to wait. Written down, this week's compelling idea competes on equal terms with last month's, and most lose their urgency in the queue — which is the queue quietly doing triage. The second job is honest prioritisation: items ranked by plausible mechanism and cost to test, not by recency or excitement.

A disciplined backlog also caps work in progress. One investigation at a time, run to its definition of done, beats five running in parallel to no conclusion — and the multiple-comparisons problem means the backlog's total size is itself a statistic: the more ideas tested, the higher the bar any winner must clear.

Where people get fooled: the backlog as a graveyard of enthusiasm — hundreds of captured ideas, none run to a verdict. Capture feels like progress and is not; the backlog only earns its keep through the items that exit it with a written yes or no.
Research backlog.usage: Generally a ranked, testable queue with capture-now-test-later discipline; its exit rate matters, its size is a multiple-comparisons warning.

Negative result archive.long:
A negative result archive is the permanent record of everything tested that did not work: the strategy that failed out-of-sample, the filter that added nothing, the idea that died on contact with costs — kept deliberately, and consulted before any new test.

The archive pays three ways. It prevents re-testing: without a record, the same seductive idea returns every eighteen months wearing a new name, and the search that already failed runs again at full cost. It calibrates the significance of wins: knowing that forty variants have been tried tells you exactly how impressed to be when the forty-first looks profitable, because the more you search, the more often noise hands you a winner. And it captures the most expensive kind of knowledge — what does not work — which every trader otherwise pays to relearn privately.

Science formalised this lesson the hard way: unpublished negative results skew entire literatures optimistic, and private research has the same file-drawer problem at smaller scale.

Where people get fooled: deleting failures because they feel like clutter. A hidden failed search is a lie by omission told to your future self — the version of you who, two years from now, finds the same pattern, runs the same test, and this time gets lucky in-sample with no record left to warn them what that luck is worth.
Negative result archive.usage: Generally a permanent log of failed tests consulted before new ones; it prevents repeat searches and prices the significance of any win.
